Remember this distinction: respiratory therapists help patients breathe smoothly, while physicians treat the underlying cause. One manages equipment and function; the other manages diagnosis and medication.

This career does not suit people who fear blood or secretions, cannot tolerate intense night shifts, or become shaky under stress. The ICU moves quickly and patients are fragile, leaving no room for panic.

A common path is: respiratory therapy program -> earn a credential and begin practice -> provide inpatient/ICU therapy -> specialize in ECMO or pulmonary rehabilitation -> become a respiratory therapy director or clinical educator.
This career suits people who are careful, steady under pressure, and willing to communicate with patients and families. If you can remain calm amid alarms, you can thrive in this field.

Respiratory therapists assess and treat patients with respiratory or cardiopulmonary conditions, operate ventilators and oxygen-therapy and airway-clearance equipment, and participate in emergency care and pulmonary rehabilitation.

paragraphs: At morning handoff, review which patients were placed on ventilation overnight. During the morning, move from bed to bed adjusting parameters, suctioning secretions, and leading breathing exercises. At midday, monitor postoperative patients' oxygenation. In the afternoon, discuss weaning timing with physicians. Respond immediately when alarms sound on night shifts, with weekend rotations as well.

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), about 139,600 respiratory therapists were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to reach 156,400 by 2034, a net increase of about 16,800 jobs, with approximately 8,800 openings per year. Median annual pay was about $80,400 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace respiratory therapists, but it will take over routine adjustments. Smart ventilators already provide closed-loop ventilation and alarms, leaving routine settings to the system. Therapists are shifting from turning knobs to assessing conditions, deciding when to wean, providing pulmonary rehabilitation, and managing communication with patients and families. Standardized operators face displacement, while therapists who can assess and communicate become more valuable.

Medium-high exposure does not mean high risk. What gets replaced is the task of standard parameter adjustment, not the role of assessing conditions and making weaning decisions. Respiratory therapists who can assess and communicate become even scarcer as productivity rises.

This field suits people who combine attention to detail, composure, and communication skills. You must understand the equipment, reassure patients, and handle night shifts.

This field develops judgment at the intersection of equipment and patients. You must interpret waveforms and blood gases while reassuring older patients who resist treatment. It suits careful, steady, resilient people who find meaning in helping someone breathe again.
They tend to be helpful, investigative, and hands-on (Social S + Investigative I + Realistic R).

The occupation's greatest risk is not AI but equipment automation. Ventilators include smart alarms and closed-loop ventilation, allowing systems to take over routine parameter adjustments. Clinical judgment, weaning timing, and patient communication still require people.

No matter how smart machines become, a respiratory therapist still uses judgment, hands-on skills, and communication to decide whether to initiate ventilation, when to wean, and how to reassure an uncooperative patient. People cannot be removed entirely from the bedside.
In one sentence: the future needs respiratory therapists who can assess patients, manage weaning, and communicate, not people who only turn knobs.
